Lesson 6 · Anticipate next week

Prediction, validation, and regularization

We have described store differences and fitted relationships. The director now asks for a weekly list of stores that are likely to struggle before the next stock report arrives.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

Operations needs a short list of stores to review before next week starts. Which forecasting procedure should the team trust? We will define the prediction loss, use later development weeks to compare complete procedures, and evaluate the selected rule on the final period.

Define what a useful forecast must predict

General theory

A prediction task specifies the target, decision time, and loss

  • Target: an outcome not yet available
  • Inputs: information available when the decision is made
  • Loss: the cost assigned to each prediction miss
  • Evaluation: predictions for rows excluded from fitting

A labelled training row has both predictors X and an observed outcome Y. A live scoring row has its available predictors but awaits the outcome. Regression predicts a numerical outcome such as a rate; classification predicts a category or its probability. The forecast horizon and intended users determine what counts as an available input. This lesson predicts one week ahead for existing stores.

Squared loss gives large misses more weight than absolute loss

Write the error as observed minus predicted. Absolute loss grows proportionally with its size; squared loss grows faster. The orange example charges twice as much per point when the forecast is too low. Loss need not be symmetric. A choice of loss expresses the operating problem before it determines which model wins. Under squared loss the optimal point forecast is the conditional mean; under absolute loss it is a conditional median.

One large miss changes RMSE more than it changes MAE

MAE = mean absolute error; RMSE = square root of mean squared error
Errors (points)MAEMSERMSE
−1, +1, +42.0006.0002.449
−2, +2, +22.0004.0002.000

For the first row, absolute errors total 6 and squared errors total 18. Divide each by three, then take the square root only for RMSE. Both rows have the same MAE, but the four-point miss raises the first RMSE. MSE has squared outcome units; MAE and RMSE have the original units. Our common model-selection score is RMSE in percentage points.

Expected prediction error combines bias, variation across fits, and new noise

Expected squared error = bias² + prediction variance + noise variance

At a fixed input x, bias is the difference between the average prediction across training samples and the true conditional mean. Prediction variance describes how fitted predictions change across those samples. Noise is the new outcome’s variation around its conditional mean. A more flexible model may reduce bias while increasing variance; it cannot remove irreducible outcome noise. This expectation is not an exact decomposition of each observed residual.

Overfitting learns sample-specific variation that does not improve new predictions

Choose useful flexibility by performance outside the fitting rows
Model behaviorFitting sampleNew outcomes
Too restrictiveMisses persistent structureCan retain substantial bias
More flexibleCan reduce fitting lossMay improve or worsen loss
OverfittedCaptures sample-specific variationFails to carry that gain forward

Adding regressors to a nested OLS model cannot increase its minimized training sum of squared errors. That algebra does not apply to new rows. Overfitting occurs when fitting sample-specific variation harms generalization; underfitting misses useful structure. Validation measures the consequence for the intended prediction task rather than choosing complexity from training fit alone.

Separate fitting, selection, and evaluation

General theory

Validation must follow the information pattern of the future decision

Ordinary k-fold validation fits k models, leaving a different part out each time. It is useful when the observations can be treated as exchangeable for the task. Forecasting asks a different question: train on earlier weeks and predict later ones. The same stores can appear in both periods because the intended use is future outcomes at existing stores. Predicting entirely new stores would also require holding stores out.

The fitted procedure includes every transformation learned from the data

  • Choose target, features, candidates, and score
  • Fit preparation and model inside each training window
  • Use validation outcomes to choose the procedure
  • Refit on development data before final evaluation

Medians, scaling parameters, category rules learned from observed data, coefficients, and any target retransformation all belong to the fitted procedure. Reusing preparation learned from validation rows gives those rows a role in fitting. The final period measures the selected procedure. After evaluation, changes to the procedure call for a new evaluation period. The appendix links the pipeline guidance and the exact implementation.

Pool squared errors before taking the root of a validation score

Pooled RMSE = √[Σ n_f × RMSE_f² / Σ n_f]

A fold with more validation rows contributes more squared errors. Averaging the fold RMSEs does not produce the pooled RMSE, even when fold sizes are equal. For equal sizes, square the fold scores, average those squares, then take the square root. Choosing alpha from these same development folds is model selection; the final period supplies the subsequent evaluation of that choice.

Information criteria trade likelihood fit against parameter count

AIC = −2 log L + 2k; BIC = −2 log L + k log n

For a common response and common rows, better likelihood fit lowers the first term and extra parameters raise the penalty. Lower is better within that comparison. Count identifiable fitted parameters, including residual variance for the full Gaussian criteria used here. BIC penalizes an extra parameter more than AIC when log n exceeds two. These training criteria and later-period RMSE answer different questions; the worked example reports both.

Control flexibility with a coefficient penalty

General theory

LASSO trades squared fitting loss against the absolute size of coefficients

Minimize RSS/(2n) + α Σ|b_j|; leave the intercept unpenalized

With alpha zero the objective reduces to least squares. Increasing alpha makes a coefficient earn its place by improving fit enough to offset its penalty. The absolute-value penalty has a corner at zero, allowing some coefficients to be exactly zero. Standardizing features makes their penalty comparable across measurement units. Alpha must be chosen by validation rather than by the final outcomes.

The penalty creates an exact zero when the fitted signal is small enough

Illustration: centered y=2z, mean(z²)=1; b=max(2−α,0)
αUnpenalized slopeLASSO slope
022
0.521.5
121

320

For this one-predictor example, the objective differs from (b−2)²/2 + alpha|b| only by a constant. On the positive side its minimum moves from 2 toward zero as alpha rises. Once alpha reaches 2, zero minimizes it. The appendix shows the positive and negative cases. With correlated features, one coefficient can rise while another falls, so a whole coefficient path need not be monotone.

Standardization puts each constructed feature on its own training scale

z_j = (x_j − training mean_j) / training SD_j

First construct the declared powers and interactions, then standardize each resulting column using the training rows. A coefficient then measures rate points per one training-standard-deviation change in that constructed feature, holding the other constructed columns fixed. A product is standardized as a product column; it is not generally the product of standardized inputs. The intercept describes the prediction at all standardized inputs equal to zero.

Feature design and missing-input rules are part of the model

  • Use main terms, powers, and interactions that fit the task
  • Remove exact duplicates such as a binary variable’s square
  • Record unavailable inputs with a missingness indicator
  • Fit replacement values from training rows

For a binary variable D, D²=D, so adding its square adds no independent information. For categories, retain a documented reference level and a rule for new categories. A missing response cannot contribute supervised training loss. A missing predictor can be handled by a trained imputation rule plus an indicator, so the same procedure can score future rows. We will work that preparation step on a small copy of the retail records.

Score forecasts on the scale of the decision

General theory

Exponentiating a fitted log value does not recover an arithmetic mean

For log(1+Y): predicted Y = exp(fitted log value) × smearing factor − 1

Exponentiation is nonlinear. A global smearing factor averages exp(residual) over training rows and estimates a common retransformation correction. Here log1p handles zero rates without discarding them. Conditional changes in log-error spread can require a richer correction; compare the complete procedure on held-out rows. For the simpler log(Y) illustration, residuals −0.2 and +0.2 multiply a naive forecast of 10 by 1.0201, giving 10.201.

Compare transformed-target procedures using the same original-scale loss

  • Use identical validation rows
  • Learn retransformation inside each training fold
  • Return predictions to rate units
  • Compare the resulting RMSE in percentage points

A smaller log-scale fitting error cannot be compared directly with a rate-scale fitting error. Retransform first and evaluate the forecast that operations would receive. Likewise, a high training R² does not establish a low future prediction loss. The candidate comparison below includes both level and log1p procedures under one chronological validation design.

Place the retail inputs on the decision clock

Worked application

Five timely inputs predict the next store-week stockout rate

150 stores; target weeks 3–16; no alert use in this period
InputAvailable before target week
lag_ratePrevious week’s measured rate
lead_days, urbanStore attributes
demand_forecastTarget-week planning forecast
promotion_planAlready scheduled promotion

The outcome is 100 times unavailable product-days divided by 140 scheduled product-days. Each row predicts a target week using the previous week’s rate and plans known beforehand. The realized target-week demand, outcome, and eventual alert status are excluded. This is a weekly forecast for the same stores, not a prediction for a new region.

A complete scoring row contains inputs before it contains its outcome

Model fitted on target weeks 3–13; no week-14 outcome used in this forecast
Before week 14: S001Value
Previous-week rate8.571%
Delivery / urban4 days / 0
Demand forecast90.524
Promotion planned1
Frozen-model forecast13.032%

The forecast is 13.032%. At the end of the target week the observed rate becomes available, allowing the error to be recorded. During weeks 14–16 the fitted coefficients remain fixed while the lagged input updates each week. A later realized lag is legitimate information for the next one-week-ahead forecast.

The forecast adds an intercept and five input contributions

Sum of unrounded contributions = 13.03171% for S001, week 14
Original-unit termContribution to forecast
Intercept-0.51782
lag_rate+0.57648
lead_days+5.92645
urban+0.00000
demand_forecast+4.78062

Convert the standardized linear coefficients back to original units: divide each slope by its training standard deviation, and subtract the mean adjustments from the intercept. Multiply those slopes by the five inputs in the preceding row. Urban is zero for this store, so its contribution is zero. Summing the intercept and contributions reconstructs the forecast; rounding intermediate entries can change the last displayed digit.

Individual squared misses build the first fold’s loss

First five of 300 predictions from the additive model fitted on weeks 3–7
StoreWeekObservedPredictedSquared error
S00185.71410.86926.574

Compute error as observed minus predicted for each row, square it, and sum across all 300 validation rows. The sum is 2257.182; dividing by 300 gives 7.524. Its square root is 2.743 percentage points. The five displayed rows illustrate the arithmetic; the fold score uses all 300.

Pooling the three fold losses gives a 2.780-point validation score

√[(2.74298² + 2.90247² + 2.68954²)/3] = 2.77980

Each fold has 300 validation rows, so equal weights are appropriate for their squared scores. The arithmetic mean of the three roots is a different statistic. Store both the row errors and fold scores so the pooled result can be reconstructed and unusually difficult periods can be investigated.

Rehearse a missing forecast before using the procedure

Worked application

A training median fills a missing input while an indicator records its absence

Labelled copy: withhold S001/S002 training forecasts and S001 validation forecasts
Quality exerciseDemand inputMissing flagFilled value
S001, week 8Unavailable1106.835
Training rows10 withheld out of 750Calculated before fillMedian 106.835

The reconciled analysis inputs are complete. This separate exercise deliberately hides selected demand forecasts to practise the deployment rule; it does not alter the main model comparison. Calculate the median from the remaining training values, create an indicator before filling, then apply the saved median to missing validation values. An unchanged observed value retains a zero indicator.

The validation row uses the training mean and standard deviation unchanged

z = (106.835 − 107.173) / 11.244 = -0.030

The mean and population-standard-deviation convention here match StandardScaler. Both are calculated after training-fold imputation. Apply those same values to validation rows; do not re-standardize the validation set on its own mean. If evaluating the missing-input procedure as a new candidate, refit this entire preparation inside every fold and include the missingness flag as an input.

Make the flexible model’s complexity explicit

Worked application

The quadratic design has eighteen distinct slope features

Exclude urban² and promotion_plan² because each equals its original binary input
Feature groupCount
Five original predictors5
Squares of three continuous predictors3
Pairwise interactions among five predictors10
Total slope features18
Including intercept: mean-equation rank19

The three continuous variables are previous rate, delivery time, and the demand forecast. Include their squares and all ten distinct pairwise products. The resulting 19-column design, including the intercept, has rank 19 in development data. The additive model has five slopes and an intercept. LASSO uses this same clean 18-feature expansion before scaling.

AIC favors the quadratic fit while BIC favors the additive fit

Full Gaussian criteria on identical 1,650 development rows; k includes residual variance
Mean modelMean parametersTotal kAICBIC
Additive678068.2928106.151
Quadratic19208058.4658166.635

The quadratic model’s better likelihood offsets AIC’s smaller penalty, but not BIC’s larger penalty. These are illustrative Gaussian working-model criteria: repeated weekly records motivate chronological validation as the operating performance check. The appendix derives the full likelihood constants and counts. We select the forecasting procedure using the predeclared rolling RMSE.

Compare complete forecasting procedures on the same weeks

Worked application

The additive regression has the lowest pooled validation RMSE

Same 900 validation rows; fitting losses pool each fold’s own training rows
ProcedureValidation RMSEFitting RMSE
Mean3.6833.654
Linear regression2.7802.790
Quadratic2.8002.756
Log-linear2.7842.793
LASSO2.7822.766

The mean-rate rule is the baseline. Additive regression uses the five timely inputs. Quadratic regression uses the clean expansion. Log-linear fits log(1+rate) and applies its training smearing factor. LASSO uses the expansion with alpha selected from .001, .01, .1, and 1. The additive rule wins under the stated criterion; the small differences among the richer candidates do not demonstrate a stable ranking in all future periods.

The richer equation improves fitting error without improving later forecasts

The quadratic model lowers fitting loss because it contains the additive model’s terms. Its validation loss rises slightly. This illustrates why an improving training fit is insufficient for selection. The graph uses the actual course results, not a forced textbook U-shape. Fitting rows recur in expanding training windows; their pooled error is a description of those fits, while each validation outcome is scored once.

The log procedure is judged after returning predictions to rate units

Adjusted = (naive + 1) × training smearing factor − 1

The two candidates predict the same original rate on the same held-out rows. The level procedure wins narrowly here. A log transformation can still be useful in another setting, but its value is assessed through the actual decision loss after retransformation, not by comparing incomparable fitting scales.

Trace the penalty choice into the retained equation

Worked application

Rolling validation selects a LASSO penalty of 0.01

The four candidate penalties produce pooled scores of 0.001: 2.7961, 0.01: 2.7819, 0.1: 2.7871, 1: 3.2084 points. Alpha 0.01 minimizes this set. Standardization is refitted inside every fold. The curve reports the selection metric, not the final-period score.

Larger penalties shrink the model toward an intercept-only forecast

Follow a colored path from left to right as alpha increases. The vertical position is the coefficient of a separately standardized constructed feature. A path reaching zero removes that term at that penalty. All paths here use development rows for illustration. They do not provide an additional reason to change the penalty selected by validation.

The selected LASSO retains ten of eighteen candidate features

The selected LASSO has ten nonzero slopes under a tolerance of 1e−8. The chart shows its six largest absolute coefficients; the appendix’s saved results list all retained terms. Products and main effects should be read as components of one prediction equation. Correlated inputs can exchange signal, so selection is not a claim that these are the unique important variables.

Evaluate the frozen choice on later outcomes

Worked application

The final forecast improves on the mean-rate benchmark

450 one-week-ahead predictions; model fitted once on weeks 3–13
Final weeks 14–16RMSE (points)MAE (points)
Frozen additive model2.9632.365
Development mean forecast3.8803.164

The selected additive procedure scores 2.963 points against 3.880 for the mean benchmark. This evaluates the selection made using development data. It does not establish a treatment effect or the financial value of acting on a forecast. The same dated record should retain model version, inputs, prediction, later outcome, and action.

Points above the diagonal reveal weeks when the model underpredicted stockouts

Read vertical distance from the diagonal as observed minus predicted. Points above it have more stockouts than forecast; points below have fewer. Inspect where misses concentrate across the forecast range and return to the corresponding operating records. Prediction intervals and their targets were developed in Lesson 5; this plot evaluates point predictions.

Track both error size and average underprediction across weeks

Mean error = observed − predicted; positive means average underprediction

Save both overall accuracy and error by period. Before extending to alert use, assign the operations analyst a weekly review: compare the newest errors with this evaluation period, inspect missing inputs and changes in promotion or delivery, and investigate a sustained increase. The alert intervention changes operating conditions, so collect a new evaluation period for that policy setting.

Work through the reasoning gap

Worked application

Compare a forecast with a timely last-week benchmark

Secondary retrospective check: five stores in each of weeks 14–16
Frozen ruleFinal RMSEReview slotsStockout days in queue
model2.9615352
lag_only4.1615305

The original selection used rolling-validation RMSE and remains fixed. Last week’s rate is a timely benchmark requiring no new fitted coefficients. Rank each week using only the available forecast, break ties by store ID, and compare on the same 15 review slots. This added check was developed after the final outcomes were available, so it is exploratory. Predeclare the queue metric and evaluate a new future period before adopting a new ranking rule.

Burden captured measures review coverage rather than prevented harm

Both rules consume the same five reviews per week
RuleQueue mean rateShare of all stockout days
model16.76%4.85%
lag_only14.52%4.20%

A queue capturing more burden locates problems efficiently at this capacity. It does not say the response prevents them. Measure staff time, actions, stockouts prevented by a credible experiment, and the value per prevented event. A risk score ranks expected outcomes under the observed policy; a treatment policy requires expected improvement under a different action. A high-risk store can be difficult to help.

Repeated fitted samples separate bias from prediction variability

Separate simulation: true mean X², noise variance 1, 500 independent training outcomes
Model at X=0Squared biasFit varianceExpected new loss
1 degree2.170.053.22
2 degree0.000.111.11

Each repetition holds 20 training X values fixed but draws new independent errors and refits. At X=0 the true mean is zero. The squared average prediction estimates squared bias; the spread across predictions estimates fitting variance. Add the known new-outcome noise variance 1 to obtain estimated expected squared prediction loss. These are Monte Carlo approximations for this design, not properties inferred from the single retail fit.

Use forecasts to allocate a finite review capacity

Worked application

Rank stores by forecasts made before the operating week starts

Illustration: review the five highest forecasts at the end of week 15

The list uses predictions, not observed week-16 outcomes. A capacity of five is an explicit operating choice: managers review products at those stores and record the time, response, and benefit. Changing the number reviewed changes workload and the possible value of the process. The model supplies a ranking; the team supplies the action and capacity rule.

A useful forecast leads to an action whose effect can be tested

  • Version and log the weekly prediction procedure
  • Assign review capacity and record the response
  • Monitor prediction loss and operating changes
  • Use Lesson 7 to evaluate whether alerts improve outcomes

Reliable forecasting answers where problems are likely to arise. Whether replenishment alerts reduce those problems is a separate question about the response. The next lesson tests that response using random assignment. Carry the forecast contract and monitoring record forward so prediction and intervention evaluation remain connected.

Explain, reconstruct, diagnose and transfer

Decision and synthesis

Reconstruct the calculation before inspecting the worked answer

  • Compare the frozen model and last-week rate using final RMSE and five reviews per week.
  • The rule locating the most stockouts must also produce the greatest alert benefit. Explain the missing causal and cost information.

Work independently or explain your reasoning to a partner. State the target, units and assumptions before calculating. The student notebook provides runnable setup and separate task cells; the companion solution checks the calculation. The lesson’s completed lab remains available as a reference, with its steps separated into smaller cells.

Transfer the method and defend the decision

  • A hospital can review five patients daily. Define a dated input, a capacity-matched evaluation measure, and a separate design to test whether review helps.
  • Submit a calculation, an assumption and a justified next action

An acceptable answer can recommend more information, a narrower claim or no action. It must connect the method to the target and explain the consequence of a failed assumption. Use the assessment criteria after attempting the task; matching a supplied recommendation is not the grading objective.

After your attempt: check the reasoning

Open the assessment criteria

Use identical held-out weeks and 15 review slots. Report burden captured and workload. Do not select a new model using the final period or call captured burden prevented harm.

Update the decision memo

Use Linear regression selected by common rolling validation. Its final RMSE is 2.963 points versus 3.880 for the mean-rate benchmark. Freeze the weekly input contract, allocate review capacity, and evaluate whether the subsequent alert action improves outcomes.

Make the call

The quadratic model lowers training RMSE but raises validation RMSE. Which rule should operations choose under the stated criterion?

Compare your reasoning

Choose the additive model by its lower rolling-validation RMSE, refit it on development rows, and evaluate that frozen procedure on the final period. Extra terms earning a better training fit is not sufficient evidence of better forecasts.

The bigger picture

Forecasting demand, cost, or service pressure uses the same sequence: define the prediction task, construct information available at the decision time, select a procedure using validation, and evaluate it on genuinely held-out observations. The value comes from reliable future performance and the action it supports.

After your decision: open the known answer

Future demand and shelf availability contain new random variation. The generator stores that variation, but the five forecast inputs expose only information available at the weekly decision time.
